Chapter 6: The Deeper Dynamics — Why Games Persist and How They Shape Identity.
As we dig a little deeper into this framework, you start to see something interesting—psychological games aren’t just habits on the surface. They’re actually woven right into our sense of self, and even our identity.
Ever wonder why some games just won’t go away? It turns out, they stick around because they serve a hidden psychological purpose. Sometimes, these games give us a sense of safety, predictability, or even a feeling of belonging—no matter how uncomfortable they might be. For a lot of people, that familiar discomfort can feel safer than stepping into the unknown with real change.
At the heart of this, you’ll find something called a “life script.” Picture a script like a well-worn path through the woods—it’s always easier to walk the same trail, even if you know exactly where it leads, rather than blaze a brand new one.
Life scripts are these unconscious patterns we pick up as kids. They shape how we expect our lives and our relationships to unfold. And the games we play? They’re just the day-to-day ways we act out those deeper scripts.
Here’s a real-world example: Imagine someone who grew up feeling overlooked. Without even realizing it, they might seek out situations where they’re ignored—or maybe even push people to dismiss them—just to confirm what they already believe about themselves. The payoff? It’s that sense of consistency with their self-image, even if it stings. In this way, games keep the script—and the identity attached to it—alive.
You can think of this dynamic as a loop:
First, there’s the script expectation—a belief or story you hold about yourself or others. Then comes the game invitation—a comment or behavior that sets everything in motion. Next is the predictable response—other people react in a way that fits your script. And finally, there’s the emotional payoff: that all-too-familiar feeling, even if it’s negative, that proves the script right once again.
So, how do you break out of this loop? Well, it takes both awareness and courage. It means being willing to question some of those old beliefs about yourself, and to sit with the discomfort that comes with trying something new—even if it feels awkward at first. It’s not a quick fix. Rewriting your script is all about small, steady changes—one interaction at a time.
Here’s a practical way you can start to shift these deeper dynamics:
First, take some time to reflect on the patterns you notice. What games keep showing up in your life? Next, think about your early influences. How might your childhood experiences have shaped the script you’re living out today?
Then, try testing out a new response when you catch yourself in a familiar game. Just see what happens. And don’t be afraid to seek support—sometimes talking things through with a trusted friend, mentor, or even a professional can help you spot things that are tough to see on your own.
By getting curious about the deeper roots of these games, you can start to loosen their hold and open yourself up to more genuine, fulfilling ways of connecting with others.
